title: ExpGuard: Domain-Specific LLM Safety
one_liner: A guardrail model trained on domain-specific harmful prompts catches specialized jargon dangers that generic models miss.
lead: Banks, hospitals, and law firms use AI assistants with specialized vocabulary. But off-the-shelf guardrails are trained on general chats and conversations, not domain jargon. A doctor saying 'diuretic' or a lawyer saying 'novation' passes through as innocent text. ExpGuard is trained specifically on harmful prompts from finance, medicine, and law, teaching it to spot when those words are being used to ask for something dangerous.

problem.h2: Generic guardrails fail on specialized words
paras: Today's AI safety systems learn from millions of everyday online conversations. A guardrail is a neural network trained to spot when a question is dangerous (asking for bomb instructions) or safe (asking for cake recipes).

But they break completely in specialized fields. In finance, a guardrail sees 'pump and dump' (a real investment crime) as three harmless words. In medicine, 'enema' is treated like normal speech. A lawyer asks about 'contract fraud' and the guardrail thinks it is a homework question. The specialized vocabulary of these fields is invisible to a model trained only on Reddit and Twitter.

A beginner might try to patch this by adding more conversations to the training data. But real harm in finance or medicine uses thousands of technical terms. You cannot collect dangerous prompts in every field — and you should not ask experts to write them by hand.

callout.html: Train a guardrail model on domain-specific harmful prompt examples (generated using the real vocabulary of that field) so it learns to spot danger when specialists use their own language.

steps.text: For each domain (finance, medical, law), pull technical terms from Wikipedia.
For each term, use GPT-4 to write a realistic prompt that asks for something harmful.
Three different LLMs look at each prompt, reason through it, and vote on safe vs. unsafe.
Humans with domain expertise review the hardest cases and correct errors.
Feed this dataset to a small LLM; it learns to classify harmful vs. safe prompts in specialized language.

paras: The paper changes the training dataset: instead of generic chats, it builds labeled examples of harmful and safe prompts in specialized fields. The guardrail model itself stays a standard classifier, but its training diet is now domain-aware.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Domain-specificity of harm
hidden.name: domain-specificity score
paras: The paper identifies something that generic datasets miss: harmful prompts in each field use vocabulary unique to that field. A prompt about 'pump and dump' is meaningless to someone without financial knowledge, but it signals fraud to a banker. The paper names this idea by collecting prompts that are harmful only when you know the domain's vocabulary.

The paper estimates domain-specificity by generating adversarial prompts using domain-specific terminology and measuring how much better a model trained on those prompts performs. It counts this in two ways: (1) how many domain-specific harmful prompts does the retrained guardrail catch, (2) how much do generic benchmarks still score, showing the method does not over-fit to one domain.

heat.caption: Darker means more domain-specific harm markers. Domain terms (top) appear in harmful prompts; generic words (bottom) do not.

reads.html: Domain-specificity is the idea that harm looks different depending on what field you are in. Medicine uses different dangerous words than banking.

The paper measures domain-specificity by showing that a guardrail trained on domain-specific terminology and adversarial examples catches 8.9% more prompt-level harms and 15.3% more response-level harms than generic guardrails, and it generalizes to unseen public benchmarks.

mechanism.h2: Why learning domain vocabulary catches domain-specific harm
paras: A guardrail is trained to take a prompt as input and output a score: this is either safe or unsafe. A model trained on generic text learns patterns like 'asking for a bomb recipe is bad' and 'asking for cake is good.' But it never sees 'pump and dump' paired with 'bad,' so it has no pattern to recognize.

When ExpGuard is trained on prompts containing domain vocabulary labeled as harmful or safe, the model builds new internal patterns. It learns 'when I see pump, dump, shares, market in the same prompt, flag it as risky.' It learns 'when I see diuretic, kidney, dose, overdose together, this is a medical danger signal.' These patterns are invisible to a generic guardrail.

The mechanism works because the model is learning to recognize that domain-specific word combinations have meaning only to someone in that field. The same words in isolation are harmless; together and in context, they point to real domain-specific crimes or harms. By training on examples, the model internalizes these combinations and can catch them in new prompts it has never seen before.

stages.s: Prompt with domain vocabulary (e.g., pump, dump, stock price)
Convert to number lists, using patterns learned from domain harms
Attention: which word patterns matter in this domain?

math.words: score = dot product of (prompt embeddings) and (learned domain-specific weight matrix), then threshold
symbols: turn the text prompt into a list of numbers that capture its meaning
learned weights tuned to recognize domain-specific harmful patterns in this field
a small constant that shifts the score
a function (S-shaped curve) that converts the score into a probability between 0 and 1
the model's final confidence that this prompt is unsafe

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Prompt 1: 'Explain how to pump and dump stock' encodes to [0.8, 0.6, 0.7, 0.5, ...] (domain vocab recognized).
Prompt 2: 'What is pump and dump?' encodes to [0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, ...] (neutral word order).
Sigmoid(0.8) ≈ 0.69 (69% confidence it is unsafe). Same words, different order, lower risk.

math.note: The W_domain table learns which word combinations signal harm in that field. The sigmoid squashes the score into a probability; the model flags any score above 0.5 as unsafe.

charts.title: Generic guardrail
charts.note: A model trained on general data misses most domain-specific harms (60%), even though it performs well on public benchmarks.

charts.title: ExpGuard (domain-trained)
charts.note: Training on domain vocabulary lifts domain-specific accuracy by 25+ points. Public benchmarks drop slightly (the model specializes), but domain harm detection soars.

items.html: If the model trains only on finance harms and never sees medical ones, it will miss medical danger. The fix: train on all three domains together, and test generalization to unseen public benchmarks.

New terms emerge in each field faster than a static dataset captures them, because criminals and fraudsters invent new schemes using fresh slang (e.g., new cryptocurrency scams with unique jargon emerge monthly). The fix: the paper describes how to retrain on new vocabulary, but a live system needs continuous updates.

The current dataset is English only. Fraudsters in other languages use domain-specific jargon too, but the model has never learned those patterns. The paper acknowledges this and leaves multilingual extension as future work.

Using three LLMs to label each prompt and checking their reasoning (chain-of-thought) catches cases where one model is wrong. Cohen's Kappa agreement is 0.89 for prompts and 0.98 for responses, showing three labelers almost always agree.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a guardrail classifier on the ExpGuardTrain dataset (or a subset). Split it into a domain set and a generic set. Train one model on generic prompts only, and another on domain-specific prompts only. Test both on (1) domain-specific adversarial prompts (unseen), (2) generic public benchmarks (WildGuard, DAN, others). Measure accuracy for both.
demo.metric_eq: domain_catch_rate = number of domain-specific harms flagged / total domain-specific harmful prompts
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: the domain-trained model catches domain harms that generic models let through, even though both do well on generic benchmarks.
